abstract: Genetic association studies have identified hundreds of largely noncoding loci associated with interindividual differences in the structure of the human cortex, although the specific functional variants contributing to these phenotypes are unknown. Here we implemented a massively parallel reporter assay to measure the regulatory activity of 9,092 cortical-structure-associated variants in human neural progenitor cells at baseline and during Wnt stimulation. We identified 918 variants with regulatory potential from 150 cortical-structure-associated loci (76% of loci studied), of which more than 50% showed allelic effects. Wnt stimulation modified regulatory activity at a subset of loci, revealing condition-dependent enhancers. Massively parallel reporter assay activity was largely induced by Alu elements, suggesting that they contribute to cortical expansion. The region-specific impact of motif-disrupting variants is probably mediated by spatially localized transcription factor expression during development. Together, these results provide a genome-scale functional framework for understanding how noncoding variation influences cortical structure.

title: Reconciling global collaboration and data sovereignty in neuroscience
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) elevates the economic and strategic value of data, governments are intensifying efforts to regulate the collection, use and cross-border transfer of personal information. Data are increasingly treated as national assets, subject to legal, economic and geopolitical controls. These shifts are reshaping scientific research, particularly in neuroscience and brain health, where progress depends on access to large, diverse and internationally distributed datasets. In parallel, advances in neuroimaging, neurotechnology and computational modeling are enabling population-scale neuroscience and the generation of AI-ready brain datasets. These developments further increase the strategic importance of neural data, amplifying both their scientific value and their governance complexity. The convergence of these trends exposes a fundamental tension between the need for an open science culture and data sovereignty. Without coordinated responses, these dynamics risk limiting representation, slowing innovation and reinforcing global inequities in brain health research. Here we argue that neuroscience requires an international data governance coordinating body capable of aligning research and regulatory priorities. In addition to outlining the distinct challenges posed by neural data, we propose strategies to support secure, equitable and sustainable global collaboration, as well as practical governance instruments to enable coordinated implementation across jurisdictions.

title: Author Correction: Synaptic-like transmission between neural axons and arteriolar smooth muscle cells drives cerebral neurovascular coupling
abstract: In the version of this article initially published, errors were identified in Fig. 1h, j and k , Fig. 8d , associated Source Data files, the Fig. 1 legend and the legend to Supplementary Fig. 4g. The total number of neurovascular smooth muscle junctions (NsMJs) reported in Fig. 1h was corrected from 502 to 499, following the removal of duplicate counts and inclusion of omitted NsMJs. In Fig. 1j , prejunctional boutons were reclassified into three categories based on vesicle content, and the Results text was revised from stating that 80% of NsMJs contained small vesicles and 20% contained dense-core vesicles to stating that 76.4% contained small vesicles only, 16.0% contained dense-core vesicles only and 7.6% contained both. In Fig. 1k , duplicated measurements were removed, resulting in a revision of the reported mean bouton-to-aSMC membrane distance from 200 nm to 205.6 nm. The Fig. 1 legend was updated to clarify sample sizes. In Fig. 8d , duplicated neural signal data were removed and the figure legend revised accordingly. The legend of Supplementary Fig. 4g was amended to clarify that the image shown was a 90° counterclockwise rotation of the image in Extended Data Fig. 4b. The figures, legends, Source Data, text and Supplementary Information have been updated in the HTML and PDF versions of the article. For comparisons, the original figures are available as Supplementary Information accompanying this amendment. These changes do not affect the conclusions of the study.

title: Comprehensive profiling of brain dynamics during anesthesia across phylogeny
abstract: The behavioral effects of anesthetics are highly conserved across species, hinting at shared and fundamental underlying mechanisms. Here we compile a dataset of multiscale neural activity during wakefulness and anesthesia, encompassing human, macaque, marmoset, mouse, zebrafish and nematode. Applying massive feature extraction, we characterize local neural dynamics across >6,000 time-series features. This reveals a conserved dynamical profile of anesthesia across species, characterized by shorter intrinsic timescales of neural activity and dampened inter-regional synchrony. Deep-brain stimulation of the macaque centromedian thalamus reverses this profile and restores behavioral responsiveness. This conserved dynamical phenotype covaries with conserved transcriptional profiles of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission. Biophysical modeling provides a potential mechanistic link between the macroscale dynamical phenotype of anesthesia and microscale effects of key molecular targets on the timescales of synaptic excitation and inhibition. These analyses reveal a shared neural endpoint of anesthesia: across species and scales, anesthetics induce spatiotemporal isolation of local neural activity.

title: A neural architecture for imagined and overt speech motor dynamics
abstract: Mental imagery is a hallmark of human cognition, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. Speech imagery (the internal simulation of speech without overt articulation) has been proposed to partially share substrates with speech production, but its spatiotemporal dynamics remain controversial. Here, we leveraged high-resolution electrocorticography to investigate shared and modality-specific coding of articulatory kinematic trajectories during speech imagery and articulation. Linear modeling revealed robust articulatory kinematic trajectories encoding in frontoparietal cortex across modalities. Supramodal populations across middle premotor, subcentral and postcentral–supramarginal regions exhibited spatiotemporal stability during integrative planning. In contrast, modality-specific populations for speech imagery and articulation were somatotopically interleaved in primary sensorimotor cortex, revealing a distinct spatiotemporal organization. We further developed a generalized decoding framework that achieved high prediction accuracy for speech imagery (median 80.4%; chance 16.7%), comparable to speech articulation (78.3%). These findings uncover a somato-cognitive organization linking supramodal planning with modality-specific representations, informing imagery-based brain–computer interfaces.

title: Conserved neural dynamics of anesthesia and the oblivion of species
abstract: General anesthetics seem to work in all living species. This raises the question of whether there are common changes in neural activity that occur during transitions between wakefulness and anesthesia. A landmark study by Luppi and colleagues now reveals a conserved dynamic signature of anesthesia that spans hundreds of millions of years of evolution.

title: CLOK: a chemigenetic multicolor labeling system to visualize neuronal birthdate and circuit integration
abstract: Understanding how neurons integrate into developing circuits and contribute to functional activity is essential for decoding brain development and plasticity. However, current methods to study neuronal integration often suffer from low throughput, limited spatiotemporal resolution or invasive procedures. To overcome these challenges, here we present CLOK, an in vivo birthdate-labeling strategy based on HaloTag technology and its broad palette of fluorescent ligands. We show that CLOK enables precise color-coding of neurons and their subcellular structures by birthdate and allows tracking of functional maturation of newborn neurons in the developing zebrafish visual and motor systems, revealing distinct maturation trajectories of early- and late-born neurons. We further demonstrate the versatility of this approach by coupling it to optical tools enabling age-specific multicolor calcium and voltage imaging, as well as optogenetic manipulation. Altogether, CLOK provides a powerful and flexible tool for optical interrogation of neuronal circuit maturation in a growing and behaving vertebrate.

title: A population code for semantics in human hippocampus
abstract: Motivated by the successes of large language models (LLMs), we hypothesized that semantic information in the brain may be expressed in distributed patterns of neural activity. We recorded responses of hippocampal neurons while individuals listened to narrative speech. Here, using an encoding model approach, we find robust encoding of semantics, even after controlling for phonemics and grammar. Individual words had complex selectivities that included multiple words in multiple semantic categories. Similar to embedding vectors in LLMs, distance between neural population responses correlated with semantic distance. For semantically similar words, even contextual embedders showed an inverse correlation between semantic and neural distances; we attribute this pattern to the noise-mitigating benefits of contrastive coding. Finally, neural population activity aligned most closely with GPT-2 embeddings, and variation in response patterns correlated with LLM-derived polysemy measures, indicating that semantic encoding is largely contextualized. Ultimately, these results provide a neurocomputational account for understanding how hippocampal neurons encode word meaning during language listening.

title: A human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived spheroid model to investigate myelin injury and repair
abstract: There are no currently approved therapies that promote new myelin formation after myelin damage, which can, in part, be attributed to a lack of reliable systems that can reproducibly model these processes. Here we engineered a human iPSC-derived spheroid model enriched with mature, myelinating oligodendrocytes and functionally reactive microglia. This model enables the study of human central nervous system remyelination after a demyelinating insult by recapitulating processes of myelin damage and repair. These include myelin fragmentation, microglial reactivity and phagocytosis of myelin debris, oligodendrocyte generation and differentiation, and axonal ensheathment with newly formed myelin. We show that newly generated oligodendrocytes contribute to remyelination, and use ultrastructural quantification to demonstrate that remyelinated axons are ensheathed by thinner myelin after injury. Altogether, we provide a model to interrogate otherwise inaccessible aspects of human myelin biology relevant to multiple sclerosis, providing mechanistic insights into disease pathways and a platform for drug screening.

title: In conversation with Sergey Stavisky
abstract: As part of our special issue on Neurotechnology, we spoke with Sergey Stavisky, Associate Professor at the University of California, Davis, about the breakthroughs that have transformed speech neuroprostheses from proof-of-concept demonstrations into practical communication systems. He reflects on the scientific surprises, engineering challenges and ethical questions that are shaping the future of neural interfaces.

title: Brain stimulation boosts CSF flow
In conversation with Jennifer Collinger
abstract: As part of our special issue on neurotechnology, we spoke with Jennifer Collinger, Professor at the University of Pittsburgh, about how sensory feedback is reshaping brain–computer interfaces, the surprising stability of neural representations after spinal cord injury, and the scientific and engineering challenges of building truly bidirectional neuroprosthetic systems that restore movement and touch.

title: WHOLISTIC tracks the entire body
The many interfaces of neurotechnology
abstract: At the heart of neurotechnology are interactions between brains and machines, users and devices, and basic and translational science. The contributions in this issue show how these interfaces are driving both technology and new discoveries about the nervous system.

title: In conversation with Edward Chang
abstract: As part of our special issue on neurotechnology, we spoke with Edward Chang, Margaret Liu Collins and Edward B. Collins distinguished Professor and Chair of neurosurgery at the University of California, San Francisco, about the evolution of speech brain–computer interfaces (BCIs). He discusses how advances in AI are accelerating the translation of BCIs into the clinic, the challenge of restoring natural communication, and why large-scale neural datasets may ultimately help build computational models of the human brain.

title: In conversation with Miguel Nicolelis
abstract: As part of our special issue on neurotechnology, we spoke with Miguel Nicolelis, Professor Emeritus at Duke University and founder of the Edmond and Lily Safra International Neuroscience Institute, about the bold ideas that have defined his career, from helping to pioneer brain–machine interfaces to establishing a neuroscience institute in northeastern Brazil with the goal of driving social transformation. He considers the scientific discoveries, technological hurdles and ethical questions that continue to shape the future of neural interfaces and neurorehabilitation.

title: Embeddedness under psilocybin
In conversation with Grégoire Courtine
abstract: As part of our special issue on neurotechnology, we spoke with Grégoire Courtine, professor at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, about spinal stimulation, brain–spine interfaces and the overlooked computational power of the spinal cord. He reflects on the experiment that convinced him paralysis was not necessarily irreversible and the potential of neurotechnology for fundamental neuroscience as much as clinical interventions.

title: Different functional connectivity gradients reflect aging and Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Aging and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) are accompanied by alterations to large-scale communication patterns in the brain, which can be tracked in vivo using functional connectivity. The location, direction and relevance of these changes remain widely debated, although they are rarely studied in the context of whole-cortex communication dynamics. Here, in two independent cohorts (BioFINDER-2, N = 973; Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, N = 129), we show that functional connectivity changes associated with aging and AD are strongly aligned with separate fundamental axes of hierarchical brain communication. Early accumulation of AD pathology and subsequent cognitive decline are both linked to functional change along the sensory–association axis. Meanwhile, age-related functional changes occur along the representation–executive axis consistently throughout the adult lifespan. These findings together suggest that both AD and aging alter major but orthogonal functional pathways in the brain. More broadly, our findings position whole-brain connectivity dynamics as a unifying framework for interpreting functional changes across the adult lifespan.

title: In conversation with Richard Andersen
abstract: As part of our special issue on neurotechnology, we spoke with Richard Andersen, James G. Boswell Professor of Neuroscience at Caltech, about the discoveries that helped to establish the posterior parietal cortex as a key hub for intention and action planning. He looks back on decades of discoveries in the posterior parietal cortex and discusses how advances in neural recording, decoding and computation are reshaping our understanding of cognition.

title: Glioblastoma treatment gels
Human claustrum neurons encode uncertainty and prediction errors during aversive learning
abstract: Flexible behavior depends on continuous updating of internal models, yet the neural circuits coordinating this process remain poorly understood. The claustrum, which is reciprocally connected to nearly the entire neocortex, is uniquely positioned to influence cortical processing. Here we report single-neuron recordings from the human claustrum during aversive learning, with anterior cingulate cortex and amygdala recordings for comparison. Claustrum and anterior cingulate neurons displayed structured, task-related responses. Distinct subpopulations encoded stimulus onset and action-contingent outcomes, with outcome representations diverging between regions. Critically, both regions encoded model-derived latent variables, including uncertainty and prediction error, but with different temporal profiles; only the anterior cingulate carried uncertainty signals during the intertrial period, whereas both regions encoded uncertainty and prediction error during the active-avoidance period. By contrast, the amygdala showed minimal latent-variable modulation. These findings provide evidence that human claustrum neurons track higher-order cognitive variables not directly observable from sensory input and reveal dissociable roles for the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex in tracking latent task states.

title: Publisher Correction: A population code for semantics in human hippocampus
Modality-specific reactive and predictive responses in the human superior colliculus
abstract: Inspired by recent theoretical work emphasizing predictive neural processing, we tested whether a midbrain structure for multimodal sensory integration—the superior colliculus—would show predictive responses to both visual and somatosensory stimulation. A multi-stage experimental design allowed us to test predictive activity in the human superior colliculus while 7-Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) allowed us to map its sensory response across superior colliculus layers ( N = 80). As expected from non-human animal work, visual and somatosensory stimulation elicited distinct depth-dependent responses. We also observed a predictive response: these same modality-specific and depth-dependent effects occurred during task periods preceding direct stimulation, when sensorimotor input was identical between visual and somatosensory conditions. Further analyses rule out cross-trial carryover and show corresponding effects in the thalamic sensory nuclei. Here our results confirm that, in humans, the superior colliculus is sensitive to both visual and somatosensory input, and they demonstrate that it carries predictive signals for upcoming sensory events.

title: Astrocytes regulate axonal mitochondrial transport deficits in C9ORF72 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis motor neurons
abstract: Disrupted axonal transport and astrocyte dysfunction are implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Here we show these processes are linked—human-induced pluripotent stem-cell-derived astrocytes carrying the C9ORF72 mutation disrupt mitochondrial axonal transport and mitochondrial function in cocultured motor neurons (MNs). Conversely, isogenic gene-corrected astrocytes or boosting astrocytic mitochondrial bioenergetics rescue axonal mitochondrial transport deficits in C9ORF72 MNs. Our results delineate a non-cell-autonomous role for astrocytes in regulating mitochondrial transport along axons in ALS models.

title: Alzheimer’s disease target and drug discovery by leveraging multiomics and electronic health data
abstract: Despite prolific genomic data from individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), translation into treatments has lagged. Here we applied Mendelian randomization to multiple AD genome-wide association studies and functional multiomics datasets to nominate druggable targets, identifying 19 targets for individuals of European ancestry and 7 for African ancestry. This included epoxide hydrolase 2 ( EPHX2 ), for which we identified a protective missense variant (p.Arg287Gln). Experiments in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons and cerebral organoids from patients with AD validated the protective role of p.Arg287Gln via reduced levels of EPHX2 and phosphorylated tau (pTau-181). Pharmacological inhibition of EPHX2 improved cognitive performance in the 5xFAD mouse model of AD. Finally, by leveraging electronic health data from 111,680 patients with mild cognitive impairment, we identified 12 drugs associated with reduced AD incidence, including trazodone (targeting ADRA1A) and baclofen (targeting GABBR1). Thus, integrating multiomics data, functional validation and electronic health data identifies new approaches for treating AD.

title: Alus harbor genetic variants that shape the human cortex
abstract: The genetic changes associated with development of the human cortex are difficult to test functionally, especially in the context of gene regulation. In this issue, Matoba et al. show that variants that shape human cortical structure are hiding inside Alu transposable elements, co-opting their inbuilt machinery to rewire regulatory networks in the developing brain.

title: Investigating molecular and hemodynamic effects of LSD in the human brain
abstract: Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) is a potent psychedelic with increasing therapeutic interest, yet qualification of target engagement using in vivo neuroimaging has not yet been performed. Using simultaneous positron emission tomography–magnetic resonance imaging technology, we describe multiple brain actions of LSD in seven healthy volunteers blinded to LSD dose received. Here we show that LSD occupies 5-HT2AR with a high affinity and increases both global cerebral blood flow (CBF) and internal carotid artery flow. LSD also decreases global connectivity, which was negatively associated with changes in CBF. We observe an anticlockwise hysteresis loop between plasma drug levels and subjective effects, suggesting atypical pharmacodynamic mechanisms. We contrast our CBF and global connectivity findings and their relation in a separate cohort of 25 participants administered psilocybin, highlighting key consistencies and differences. By establishing the dose–occupancy relation of LSD in humans, our findings provide insights for the clinical development of psychedelic compounds and demonstrate unique neurophysiological effects that distinguish LSD from psilocybin.

title: Genome-wide analysis of common structural variants in Alzheimer’s disease identifies a risk-associated regulatory CCG repeat in FAM193B
abstract: Although Alzheimer’s disease (AD) has a polygenic architecture, with numerous associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) identified, the contribution of structural variants (SVs) is unclear. In this study, using long-read ( n = 11) and short-read ( n = 3,190) sequencing data from the Chinese population, we show that common SVs contribute to AD heritability beyond common SNPs. We identify an expanded CCG repeat in the FAM193B promoter that shows a genome-wide significant association with increased AD risk (odds ratio = 2.20 per 10-repeat increase, P = 5.5 × 10 −13 ). The expanded FAM193B -CCG repeat increases FAM193B expression and mediates the pleiotropic association between brain FAM193B expression and AD risk. Analyses of postmortem human brains and cultured neuronal cells show that elevated neuronal FAM193B expression is associated with DNA damage and cell death-related pathways. These findings establish the common FAM193B -CCG repeat as an AD risk genetic factor and highlight the contribution of common SVs to AD heritability.

title: Author Correction: T cell-mediated microglial activation triggers myelin pathology in a mouse model of amyloidosis
abstract: In the version of this article initially published, the Source Data for Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 10b contained values from an internal working file used to validate tracking rather than the final analysis. In addition, the Source Data files for Extended Data Figs. 2–7 retained figure labels from an earlier version of the manuscript. The affected Source Data files have been replaced, Fig. 1h has been updated, the figure labels have been corrected, and the legend of Extended Data Fig. 10 has been revised to report the correct sample sizes. These corrections do not affect the conclusions of the study. For comparison, the original Fig. 1 is available as Supplementary Information accompanying this amendment.

title: Symmetries and continuous attractors in disordered neural circuits
abstract: A core challenge in neuroscience is reconciling idealized models with experimental data. Classical continuous-attractor models describe neural representations of continuous variables such as head direction. Symmetry in the weights generates a manifold of stable states, with tuning curves identical up to shifts. Rodent head-direction cells, by contrast, are markedly heterogeneous. Such heterogeneity, we show, is nevertheless compatible with these models. Here we build, directly from head-direction cell data, recurrent networks that behave as quasicontinuous attractors. A generative process then reproduces the heterogeneous tuning of these cells while making connectivity and dynamics tractable at large N . Although the weights appear disordered, they carry a circular symmetry whose eigenvalue degeneracies could signify continuous-attractor organization in connectome data. Dynamical mean-field theory recovers the ingredients of classical ring attractors, namely, Mexican hat interactions and a spontaneously broken symmetry producing bump states. Continuous-attractor mechanisms may thus operate in complex mammalian circuits.

title: Ring attractor networks go full circle
abstract: Clark et al. demonstrate that heterogeneous data-driven models implement head-direction selectivity through the same dynamical principles as classical ring networks. In doing so, the authors reconcile biological realism with theoretical simplicity, unifying existing frameworks and broadening the space of connectivity structures to be searched in data.

title: An aging-sensitive secreted phospholipase confers neuroprotection and cognitive resilience
abstract: Cognitive reserve theory posits that compensatory mechanisms during aging stave off cognitive decline and lower risk for Alzheimer’s disease. Here, in a screen for hippocampal dentate granule cell (DGC) synapse loss-induced factors in mice, we identified a secreted phospholipase, Pla2g2f , whose expression increases in DGCs during aging and is associated with cognitive resilience in humans. Pla2g2f deletion in DGCs exacerbates aging-associated pathophysiological changes, including synapse loss, inflammatory microglia, reactive astrogliosis, impaired neurogenesis, lipid dysregulation, lipid droplet accumulation and hippocampal-dependent memory loss. Conversely, boosting Pla2g2f in DGCs during aging is sufficient to prevent these pathophysiological alterations in hippocampal–cortical circuits, protect memory and prophylactically modify trajectory of cognitive decline. Mutagenesis of the catalytic site of PLA2G2F prevented lipid droplet mobilization and reduction of reactive gliosis and inflammatory microglia. Neuronal PLA2G2F mediates intercellular signaling to decrease lipid droplet and cholesterol ester load in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Our findings implicate PLA2G2F as a compensatory neuroprotective broadcast signal that maintains lipid homeostasis to counteract aging-associated cognitive decline.

title: Periventricular gradient pathology is linked to ependymal reactivity and cell adhesion disruption in multiple sclerosis
abstract: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-adjacent brain areas are especially vulnerable to diffuse degeneration in multiple sclerosis (MS). Surface-in gradients arising from CSF-borne cytotoxic factors have been proposed to predict disease relapses independent of white matter lesions. Yet, whether such factors disrupt ependymal cells to penetrate the ventricular border in MS remains unknown. Here, using ultra-high-field magnetic resonance imaging-guided histology, electron microscopy and single-nucleus multiomics, we found that ependymal pathology correlates with periventricular gradients and involves an immune-reactive state marked by transporter and junctional protein dysregulation. We further defined the gene regulatory networks underpinning the MS ependymal state and predicted ligands known to be enriched in MS CSF that could drive the emergence of this state. One of the candidates, IFNγ, increased murine ependymal permeability in vivo, indicating that CSF ligands can modulate ependymal function and regional inflammation. These findings identify CSF-driven ependymal dysfunction as a contributor to periventricular pathology in MS.

title: A half-center oscillator regulates sleep pressure
abstract: Changes in oscillatory neural dynamics reflect—but may not necessarily determine—transitions between sleep stages and variations in sleep pressure. Here we show that sleep-control neurons innervating the dorsal fan-shaped body of Drosophila (dFBNs) produce slow-wave activity (SWA) that is causally linked to sleep. The dFBN ensemble contains bistable cells whose membrane voltages oscillate between hyperpolarized DOWN and depolarized UP states. The oscillations rely on interhemispheric competition of two half-centers connected by inhibitory glutamatergic synapses. dFBN-restricted interference with glutamate release disrupts SWA and baseline as well as rebound sleep, whereas the optogenetic replay of SWA induces sleep. dFBNs generate SWA throughout the sleep–wake cycle (despite mutual antagonism with arousing dopaminergic neurons) and adjust its power to sleep need via sleep history-dependent increases in excitability and homeostatic synaptic depression. The oscillatory format permits a continuous encoding of sleep pressure but requires mechanisms that convert the amplitude-modulated signal into binary sleep–wake states.

title: 5-HT2A receptors in layer 5 pyramidal neurons mediate the neuroplastic but not the hallucinogenic effects of psilocybin
abstract: It is unclear how serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT 2A Rs) in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons differentially contribute to psilocybin-induced hallucinations versus neuroplasticity. Here we show that psilocybin promotes synapse formation and maturation while accelerating the elimination of pre-existing synapses. Cell type-specific manipulation further demonstrated that 5-HT 2A R signaling in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons is necessary and sufficient for psilocybin-induced synaptic remodeling but dispensable for the head-twitch response, a rodent proxy of hallucination.

title: Spatiotemporal AI-based modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain using Seal
abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 regions, 30 cell types and 7 developmental stages. Seal predictions provide mechanistic interpretation by linking variants to transcriptional regulators in a spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole-genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing cell-type-specific and stage-specific effects. By connecting genetic variation to spatiotemporal regulatory programs, Seal offers a general framework for uncovering mechanisms of human brain development and disease.

title: An amygdala-mediated simulation-to-decision cascade aligns interbrain dynamics to solve social dilemmas
abstract: Mutual cooperation (MC) requires independent decision-makers to coordinate under uncertainty about each other’s intentions. Using simultaneous intracranial electroencephalography from epilepsy–patient dyads playing a real-time iterated prisoner’s dilemma, we identified neurocognitive mechanisms that enable interacting brains to align during mutual cooperation. Amygdala interbrain representational alignment (IBRA), similarity in fine-grained neural spectral patterns across partners, emerged selectively during MC and predicted trial-by-trial outcomes. Early θ-suppression-characterized IBRA reflected rapid, history-sensitive alignment, whereas later IBRA, characterized by low-frequency suppression and γ increases, supported coordinated commitment and action. Furthermore, mutual cooperation relied on an amygdala-mediated, simulation-to-decision cascade, operationalized here as a model-based prospective estimate of partner cooperation that guided self-choice. Amygdala low-frequency suppression tracked this prospective estimate of partner cooperation and θ–γ coupling linked this partner estimate to self-decision processes. Conditional cooperators strategically relied on partner tracking, whereas unconditional cooperators leveraged dispositional tolerance of uncertainty to transition into anticipatory neural alignment. These findings reveal the neural interdependency underpinning MC, redefining cooperation not as isolated decision-making but as a dynamic, interbrain, cognitive alignment.

title: Spatiotemporal remodeling in habenula marks the onset of depression-related phenotypes
abstract: Chronic stress has lasting adverse consequences that can lead, over time, to depression, yet the optimal timeframe for effective therapies remains unclear. The lateral habenula (LHb) has been implicated in stress-related behavioral repercussions, but the precise timing of its contribution is not understood. Here, using spatial transcriptomics, we generated a spatially resolved molecular atlas of the LHb of male mice, revealing a topographically organized and temporally defined remodeling of gene expression after chronic stress. Longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of individual LHb neurons revealed progressively heightened excitatory responses to aversive stimuli. These neuronal adaptations mirrored both the progression of transcriptional changes and the emergence of depression-related behavioral phenotypes and were reversed by the antidepressant ketamine. Moreover, chemogenetically limiting LHb neuronal activity or administering ketamine at the onset of these changes exerted antidepressant effects. These findings link spatiotemporal signatures of LHb neuronal ensembles and genetic landscape with the onset of stress-induced depression-related states.

title: Early lineage divergence segregates sensory and motor-associative identities in the thalamus
abstract: The thalamus integrates sensory, motor and associative functions through distinct nuclei, yet the developmental principles driving their specification remain unclear. Here we generate a spatiotemporal single-cell multiomic and spatial transcriptomic atlas of the embryonic mouse thalamus, combined with barcoding-based lineage tracing. We identify two major glutamatergic lineages, sensory-related and motor-associative, each governed by different gene regulatory programs and temporal dynamics. These lineages arise from spatially and molecularly distinct progenitor domains, revealing an early segregation of functional identities. Within the sensory lineage, we resolve branching sensory trajectories leading to first-order visual and somatosensory neurons, both emerging from a shared higher-order-like state. Using in silico predictions and in vivo perturbation, we identify Sp9 as a key regulator of visual thalamic fate. Together, our findings define the molecular architecture and developmental trajectories that underpin thalamic modality specification, providing a framework to understand how functional circuits emerge in the mammalian brain.

title: Dysregulated cholesterol trafficking through ABCA1 drives neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: Although brain cholesterol dysregulation is implicated in Parkinson’s disease (PD), targeting cholesterol synthesis has shown limited efficacy. Here we identify ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) as a critical regulator of cholesterol homeostasis in PD. We show that ABCA1 expression is elevated in the substantia nigra of postmortem PD brains and in a PD mouse model, with regional analyses revealing preferential alterations in nigral and striatal circuits. Mechanistically, astrocytic ABCA1 drives excessive cholesterol efflux in mice, promoting neuronal cholesterol overload. In neurons, ABCA1 localizes to lysosomes, where it facilitates cholesterol import, leading to cholesterol accumulation, autophagy impairment and α-synuclein pathology. Genetic silencing of Abca1 in either astrocytes or dopaminergic neurons attenuates neurodegeneration and behavioral deficits in vivo. Furthermore, we identify magnesium citrate as an ABCA1 inhibitor and show that it reduces dopaminergic neuronal loss in a PD mouse model. Our findings identify an ABCA1-dependent cholesterol pathway underlying PD pathogenesis and support ABCA1 inhibition as a potential disease-modifying strategy.

title: A corticohypothalamic circuit that mediates maternal awakening to pup cries
abstract: Maternal caregiving requires sensory vigilance to ensure offspring survival, particularly during sleep. Infant cries are salient sensory cues that reliably trigger maternal arousal and caregiving responses in both humans and dams, but the underlying neural circuitry remains poorly defined. Here we identify a corticohypothalamic circuit in mice that mediates maternal awakening in response to pup calls. We show that layer 6 (L6) neurons in the temporal association cortex and ectorhinal cortex (TeA/Ect) projecting to the preoptic area (POA) exhibit enhanced responsiveness to pup calls after the transition to motherhood. This enhanced responsiveness is mediated by increased expression of dopamine receptor D1 (Drd1) in TeA/Ect → POA neurons. Additionally, we reveal a pathway from the auditory thalamus to L6 TeA/Ect neurons that transmits pup cues during sleep. Together, these findings identify a dedicated neural circuit that grants infant cries privileged access to arousal systems, likely representing a fundamental adaptation for caregiving across mammals.

title: SIK3 controls synaptic localization of NMDA receptors by phosphorylating GluN1
abstract: Synaptic NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs) are central components of all neural computations. NMDAR levels critically vary between synapses but how the synaptic localization of NMDARs is controlled remains unclear. Here we show that SIK3, a serine–threonine protein kinase, localizes to synapses where it phosphorylates the obligatory NMDAR subunit GluN1 at a single site. This single phosphorylation event controls NMDAR recruitment to synapses. Genetic deletion of SIK3 severely and selectively decreases synaptic GluN1 levels by ~60% without altering AMPA-type glutamate receptor levels or inducing major transcriptional changes. Pharmacological inhibition of SIK3 impairs synaptic NMDAR responses within 45 minutes. Mutating the SIK3-phosphorylation site inhibits GluN1 synaptic recruitment. ‘Sleepy’, a gain-of-function mutation in SIK3 that increases sleep, selectively enhances synaptic NMDAR levels by increasing GluN1 phosphorylation. Thus, SIK3 phosphorylation of GluN1 provides a key signal for recruiting NMDARs to synapses.

title: Behavioral genomics identifies Creld1 as a cross-modal regulator of somatosensation
abstract: Somatosensation is mediated by dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, which convert physical and chemical stimuli into electrical signals. However, the full repertoire of molecular components underlying somatosensation remains incompletely identified. Here we developed an efficient postnatal CRISPR–Cas9 knockout platform for interrogating DRG-expressed genes (such as Piezo 2 , Trpv 1 and Scn9a ) in mice using AAV9-mediated single-guide RNA delivery. Combining this approach with somatosensory behavioral assays, we performed a targeted screen of 20 genes and identified Creld1 as a cross-model regulator of somatosensation. Either single-guide RNA-mediated postnatal knockout or tamoxifen-induced Cre-mediated deletion of Creld1 in DRG neurons resulted in profound behavioral deficits in touch, temperature, pain and itch, whereas its overexpression enhanced touch and thermal responses. Mechanistically, CRELD1 functions as an auxiliary regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels (Na v ) for controlling DRG neuron excitability. Together, this work establishes a robust postnatal screening platform for behavioral genomics and identifies Creld1 as a master regulator of somatosensory function.

title: Network geometry shapes the transformation of task representations across the human cortex
abstract: Flexible cognition requires the brain to generalize across tasks while preserving task-specific information. Previous work showed that task representations are compressed in the association cortex and expanded in sensory and motor systems, but the mechanisms underlying these transformations are unclear. Here we test whether the geometry of intrinsic brain connectivity constrains how representations change between cortical regions. We analyzed functional MRI acquired during 16 diverse cognitive tasks together with activity flow modeling, finding that connectivity dimensionality predicts representational changes across the cortex. Low-dimensional connectivity compressed task representations and increased similarities across tasks, whereas high-dimensional connectivity expanded representations and supported conjunctive coding of task features. Activity flow modeling reproduced the observed compression-to-expansion pattern along the sensory–association–motor hierarchy and generated representational geometries that more closely matched targets than sources, consistent with transformation rather than transfer of information. These findings identify network geometry as a systems-level principle that shapes cortical representations and supports flexible cognition.

title: Identification of candidate markers for the isolation of neuron-specific extracellular vesicles
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are present in biofluids and may be useful biomarkers to non-invasively monitor brain cells, but isolating cell type-specific EVs remains challenging. Here we introduce an approach to immuno-isolate EVs from neurons and glia based on protein surface markers. We first selected transmembrane proteins suitable as cell type-specific EV markers based on gene expression and EV proteomic data. We developed a high-purity EV isolation method and cataloged the proteins present on EVs in human cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. We then computationally identified cell type-specific candidate markers for isolating EVs from neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia. Using ultrasensitive immunoassays against several predicted neuron-specific proteins, we confirmed one marker, NRXN3, as present on EVs in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Finally, we developed efficient EV immuno-isolation methods and applied them to isolate NRXN3 + EVs. Our work provides a general methodology for the isolation of cell type-specific EVs, advancing the goal of using EVs to study brain diseases.

title: Sustained antidepressant-like effects of psychedelics through 5-HT2AR–β-arrestin signaling
abstract: Psychedelics produce long-lasting antidepressant effects, but their hallucinogenic properties limit clinical use. Using structure-guided design of 5-HT 2A R–β-arrestin-biased agonists, we identified β-arrestin signaling as a critical driver of prolonged antidepressant-like effects in mice. Here we show that the slow-dissociation kinetics of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) enable progressive accumulation of 5-HT 2A R engagement during repeated low-dose administration, approaching the receptor occupancy achieved by an acute high dose while avoiding its high peak concentration. This kinetic separation sustains β-arrestin signaling while limiting robust Gα q -mediated Ca 2+ responses. Consistent with this framework, repeated low-dose LSD and repeated low-dose psilocybin pretreatment followed by a high-dose psychedelic challenge produced sustained antidepressant-like behavioral effects in mice. In parallel, these regimens produced no detectable psychedelic-associated behavioral disruption in mice and cynomolgus macaques. Together, these findings uncover the signaling basis of sustained psychedelic efficacy and provide a rational framework for developing nonhallucinogenic psychedelic therapies for psychiatric disorders.

title: Chronic progressive demyelination induces a microglial state with lysosomal dysfunction
abstract: Dysfunctional immune responses impair remyelination and contribute to neurodegeneration. While immune and metabolic responses to acute myelin injury are well characterized, myeloid cell adaptations to chronic myelin damage remain poorly understood. Here we performed a comparative analysis of genetic and toxic mouse models of acute and chronic demyelination, which identified a distinct microglial state associated with chronic demyelination, characterized by sustained pro-inflammatory activation, lysosomal lipid sequestration and reduced lipid droplet formation. Transcriptomics profiling further revealed a metabolic program marked by upregulated cholesterol synthesis and diminished sterol efflux. Treatment with a desmosterol mimetic possessing 24-dehydrocholesterol reductase inhibitor activity reversed this microglial state, attenuated pro-inflammatory signaling (including C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 4 expression), reduced myelin damage and improved motor performance in a mouse model of leukodystrophy. Our findings uncover a pro-inflammatory microglial state characterized by lysosomal dysfunction and increased myelin reactivity, highlighting a novel therapeutic target for chronic demyelinating disorders.

title: Microglial NUS1 deficiency drives dopaminergic neurodegeneration through intercellular iron dysregulation in Parkinson’s disease models
abstract: The selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is a defining feature of Parkinson’s disease (PD), yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. NUS1 , which encodes neurite outgrowth inhibitor-B receptor (NgBR), was recently identified as a PD risk gene. Here we show that NgBR is highly expressed in microglia, where its deficiency drives progressive PD-like motor deficits and dopaminergic neurodegeneration via the LCN2–SLC22A17 iron-transport axis in mice. NgBR deficiency in mouse and human microglia triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress and PERK–ATF4–NUPR1 signaling, which preferentially induces LCN2-mediated iron efflux over cytokine release. Subsequently, microglia-derived iron-loaded Holo-LCN2, but not iron-free Apo-LCN2, is internalized by SLC22A17, a receptor highly expressed in dopaminergic neurons, leading to iron overload and ferroptosis. Pharmacological inhibition of LCN2–SLC22A17 axis or ferroptosis alleviated dopaminergic neuron loss and PD-like symptoms caused by microglial NgBR deficiency in vitro and in vivo. Our findings identify disrupted intercellular iron homeostasis as a pathological driver of PD and highlight the LCN2–SLC22A17 axis as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Stimulus-specific recruitment of human amygdala neurons predicts episodic memory encoding success
abstract: Controlling whether an experience is encoded into long-term memory and thus later remembered is a crucial aspect of memory. Here we examined single-neuron activity in the human brain while participants formed memories for novel visual stimuli and later retrieved them with confidence ratings. Category-selective amygdala neurons exhibited elevated firing during encoding of later remembered items relative to later forgotten items. This effect was predictive of the episodic aspect of the memory, was restricted to the preferred category of each cell, emerged earlier and was stronger in the amygdala compared to the hippocampus, and did not depend on stimulus valence and arousal. Successful memory formation was accompanied by enhanced spike-field coherence between the activity of amygdala category cells and hippocampal field potentials. These findings demonstrate that stimulus-specific recruitment of the amygdala predicts memory formation and suggest category cells in the right amygdala as a target for interventions to treat disorders affecting episodic memory in humans.

title: Circuit mechanisms for disentangled representations and generalization in the hippocampus
abstract: Understanding how the heterogeneous activity patterns of individual neurons give rise to coherent population dynamics and cognition is a central challenge in neuroscience. In the hippocampus, neurons are tuned to spatial location, yet their activity is also modulated by multiple external and internal variables and appears to drift randomly over time, making it difficult to link hippocampal computations to behavior. By analyzing hippocampal population dynamics in behaving mice, we reveal a structured organization underlying the diversity of single-neuron responses—the hippocampus encodes different aspects of experience as disentangled variables represented in the co-activity dynamics of cell assemblies. The temporal and contextual components of these representations are governed by local inhibitory interactions and input-driven cell–assembly dynamics, respectively. Our findings reveal the circuit basis of disentangled hippocampal representations, offering a unifying geometric principle of population coding that supports flexible memory representations and enables rapid generalization of prior knowledge to new situations.

title: Serotonin signaling enhances phagocytosis by brain macrophages through Htr2b and alleviates brain injury after stroke
abstract: Brain myeloid cells, including infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) and microglia, play critical roles in ischemic brain injury, clearing debris and shaping neuroinflammation and neurological outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, using single-cell RNA sequencing and fate mapping with an MDM-specific Ms4a3 creERT2 -Ai14 mouse line, we identified serotonin receptor Htr2b + MDMs as a crucial cell population involved in resolving neuroinflammation within the ischemic penumbra. Htr2b + MDMs significantly accumulate in the peri-infarct region and exhibit enhanced phagocytosis and inflammation-resolving gene signatures. Mechanistically, Htr2b activation promotes nuclear translocation of Tfe3, a key lysosomal regulator, enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and supporting phagocytic activity. MDM-specific Htr2b ablation impairs debris clearance, exacerbates neuroinflammation and ischemic injury, whereas pharmacological agonism or Tfe3 activation restores lysosomal biogenesis in brain MDMs and improves post-stroke outcomes. Thus we demonstrate a previously unrecognized Htr2b + MDM subset that integrates serotonin signaling to license intrinsic phagocytic function, alleviating ischemic brain injury.

title: A multi-institutional investigation of psilocybin’s effects on mouse behavior
abstract: Studies reporting the effects of psychedelic drugs on mouse behavior are rapidly emerging. However, the reproducibility and reliability of these effects remain uncertain. Here we implemented a multi-institutional collaborative approach to assess which effects of psilocybin on mouse behavior are robust and replicable. Five independent laboratories performed the same experiments to test the acute and persistent effects of psilocybin (2 mg kg −1 , intraperitoneally) on various behaviors. Psilocybin acutely increased anxiety- and avoidance-related behaviors and decreased fear expression in a robust and replicable manner. Surprisingly, however, psilocybin did not have replicable effects 24 h after administration in terms of reducing anxiety- and depression-like behaviors or facilitating fear extinction learning. Additionally, we did not observe psilocybin-induced alterations in social preference or social reward learning. Our characterization of psilocybin’s behavioral effects, using ~200 male and female mice per experiment across five laboratories, demonstrates several robust acute effects and suggests that some of psilocybin’s reported persistent effects in mice may be modest and/or inconsistent.

abstract: Single-neuron recordings provide direct evidence that the human claustrum tracks uncertainty and prediction errors during adaptive behavior. Its responses differed from those in the anterior cingulate cortex, which raises the possibility that these regions make distinct contributions to updating beliefs and guiding behavior in ever-changing environments.

title: Single-neuron encoding of rapidly learned visual information reshapes human perception
abstract: Humans can swiftly learn to recognize visual objects after minimal exposure. Integrating new information with existing knowledge requires forming enduring neuronal representations to enable future recognition. Yet, the neuronal mechanisms in the human brain underlying such rapid perceptual changes remain unclear. Here we recorded single-neuron activity in occipital cortex (OC) and medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions as participants rapidly learned to recognize degraded images. OC and MTL neurons modulated their activity to encode newly learned visual information and reshape perception. Population decoding revealed that OC neurons required additional processing time to resolve the identity of learned images, with delayed neuronal responses in the MTL. Our findings suggest that OC supports recognition after rapid learning via extensive recurrent processing, potentially involving higher-order neocortical areas, without relying on feedback from MTL. These results provide mechanistic constraints for biologically plausible models of visual recognition and few-shot visual learning.
